title: Forgiving strangers
hookLine: the driver who cut in, the rude clerk

cards: The light turns green, and a gray hatchback slides into the lane with no signal, close enough to touch. A horn goes off.
Later, at the pharmacy counter, the clerk sighs, doesn't look up, and pushes the bag across without a word. Neither knows your name. Neither will think of you again.
And yet these two can follow someone around for a whole afternoon, retold at dinner, replayed in the shower. Today belongs to the small hurts, the strangers.
Two short sayings from the Bible's wisdom books have a plan for them.

teach.b: Proverbs nineteen says, in the King James words: "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression." Deferreth: puts off, slows down. The anger isn't banned.
It's made to wait, long enough for good sense to catch up. Second, the verb: pass over. Not punish, not report, not retell at dinner.
The picture is walking past something on the road, the way the gray hatchback is already three blocks away. And the proverb doesn't call this weakness. It calls it glory.

It advises against straining to hear every word said about you, or you may hear your own servant cursing you, and it gives the reason: "For oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others."
The clerk is having a day.
So have you, and on some of those days someone else was the stranger on the receiving end. Fourth, passing over isn't pretending. Cutting someone off is still dangerous.
It just means not carrying a stranger home.
They were a stranger at breakfast; they don't need to become a roommate in your head by dinner.

how: Jews and Christians read Proverbs and Ecclesiastes among the Bible's wisdom books; Proverbs 19:11, on passing over an offense, is sometimes quoted when people talk about letting small slights go.

o: letting small hurts from passing strangers go quickly
pretending a stranger's rudeness didn't bother you
staying polite to strangers no matter what they do

games.q: two old sayings — tap the pairs.

s: Proverbs calls passing over an offense a weakness
"it is his glory to pass over a transgression."
Ecclesiastes reminds its reader that they have cursed others too
"thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others."
forgiving a stranger quickly means the rudeness was fine
it was still rude; passing over it just means not carrying it home.

games.q: a stranger snaps at you in a line. you could answer back, report them, or do something else. what does Proverbs 19:11 call glory?
games.why: "it is his glory to pass over a transgression." the anger is deferred, made to wait, and the offense is walked past.

practice: Bring back one stranger from the last few days, a driver, a caller, someone in a line, and see the moment clearly, just once.

Then let the picture widen: they woke up somewhere this morning, with a kitchen, a phone full of messages, a problem you know nothing about. You don't have to like what they did; just let them be a whole person with a whole day.
On an out-breath, let them go back to that day without you, and if you pray, you can include them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Forgiving strangers. Letting go quickly of small hurts from people you'll never meet again, without pretending they were fine. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, Proverbs 19:11: to pass over, to go by or across.

carryVoice: Your line: they're having a day. So have you, sometimes. That's day nine hundred eighty-seven.
